title: Micro-Frontends
summary: Splitting a large frontend across teams with independent deploys — build-time, run-time, and server-side composition, shared dependencies, and when the pattern isn't worth its cost.

slides.markdown:
**Micro-frontends** split one large web app into independently-built, independently-deployed pieces owned by separate teams, composed together at the browser. The pitch is the frontend equivalent of microservices: team A ships checkout on Tuesday, team B ships search on Thursday, neither waits for the other's release train.

The catch, covered honestly in this topic, is that the pattern trades deploy independence for real runtime cost — duplicated framework bundles, cross-app communication that's harder than a function call, and operational complexity that a monolithic SPA never has to think about. Knowing when this trade is worth making — and saying so unprompted — is a stronger interview answer than reciting the integration approaches.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem it solves: independent team deploys
slides.markdown:
A single large SPA owned by many teams has one build, one deploy, one release train. Shipping a one-line fix to checkout means it rides along with whatever search and profile happen to have in flight — if profile's change breaks the build, checkout's fix is blocked too, and a bad deploy takes down the whole app for every team's users at once.

Micro-frontends exist to remove that coupling: each team owns a deployable unit — often mapped to a page, a route, or a distinct UI region — that ships on its own schedule, with its own CI pipeline, and (ideally) fails in isolation rather than taking the whole app down. The organizational driver is almost always **team count and release-cadence mismatch**, not a technical limitation of a single SPA — a team of six engineers rarely needs this; an org of 40 teams sharing one app frequently does.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: build-time, run-time, and server-side composition
slides.markdown:
Three genuinely different ways to assemble independently-owned pieces into one app:

| Approach | How it works | Deploy independence | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Build-time** | Each micro-frontend published as an npm package, the shell imports and bundles them together | Weak — the shell must rebuild and redeploy to pick up a change | Simplest to reason about, closest to a normal monolith |
| **Run-time (module federation)** | Each micro-frontend deployed separately; the shell fetches and mounts its JS bundle in the browser at load time | Strong — a team ships by deploying their bundle, no shell rebuild | Shared-dependency and versioning complexity (next slide) |
| **Server-side composition** | Each fragment rendered server-side (often by its owning team's service) and stitched into one HTML response (edge-side includes, or a composing gateway) | Strong, and works without client-side JS to do the stitching | Needs server infrastructure per fragment; harder client-side interactivity across fragment boundaries |

Run-time composition via **module federation** (Webpack 5 / Vite plugins) is the default most teams reach for today because it gives real deploy independence without needing server-side infrastructure per team.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a shell composing three micro-frontends
slides.markdown:
The shell app is a thin host: routing, top-level layout, and shared chrome (nav bar, footer), with almost no feature logic of its own. At each route, it fetches and mounts the micro-frontend that owns that piece of the UI — checkout's team deploys their bundle independently, and the next page load picks it up with zero shell changes.

The key property this diagram makes visible: the shell doesn't know checkout's internals, only a mount contract ("give me a DOM node, I'll call your `mount(container)` function"). That contract is the entire coupling surface between the shell and every micro-frontend — everything on either side of it can change independently as long as the contract holds.

slides.sectionTitle: Shared dependencies: avoiding duplicate framework bundles
slides.markdown:
Naively, if checkout and search are each their own bundle and both import React, a user's page load ships **two copies of React** — bytes the user pays for twice, and two separate React instances that can't share context or hooks across the mount boundary.

Module federation's answer is **shared singletons**: the host declares which dependencies (React, a design-system package) should be shared, and federated bundles consume the host's already-loaded copy instead of bundling their own, with a version-negotiation step at load time if versions differ slightly. The trade-off is real: if checkout needs React 19 features but the shell is pinned to React 18, sharing forces a negotiation — either checkout ships its own copy for that one dependency (paying the duplication cost) or the whole org coordinates the upgrade together, which is exactly the release-train coupling micro-frontends were meant to avoid.

This is the sharp edge most teams underestimate before adopting the pattern: independence is real for app code, but shared infrastructure dependencies still need org-wide coordination.

slides.subTitle: Events, shared state, URL as contract
slides.markdown:
Two micro-frontends on the same page occasionally need to talk — checkout's mini-cart needs to know the search MFE just added an item. Since they're built and deployed independently, they can't import each other's internals; three patterns fill the gap:

- **Custom events on the DOM/window** — one MFE dispatches a `CustomEvent`, others listen. Loosely coupled (no shared code needed) but easy to make untyped and undocumented if left informal.
- **A small shared event bus or shared-state package** — a tiny, explicitly-versioned package both MFEs depend on, giving typed cross-app messages instead of stringly-typed DOM events.
- **The URL as the contract** — encode shared state (a selected filter, a cart ID) in the URL/query params, so any MFE can read it without any direct communication channel at all; the most decoupled option, but only works for state that's reasonable to put in a URL.

The rule of thumb: prefer the URL where the state is navigable and shareable, a typed shared-state package for frequent structured messages, and raw DOM events only for rare, simple signals.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: team autonomy vs consistency, bundle duplication, operational complexity
slides.markdown:
| Benefit gained | Cost incurred |
|---|---|
| Independent deploys per team | Coordinating shared dependency versions across teams |
| Teams can pick their own internal patterns/state library | Inconsistent UX/interaction patterns across MFEs if design-system usage isn't enforced |
| A bad deploy from one team can, in principle, stay isolated | In practice, requires real isolation work (error boundaries per mount, no shared global mutable state) that a monolith gets for free |
| Smaller, more comprehensible codebase per team | More total infrastructure — separate CI pipelines, separate hosting, a composition layer to maintain |

The honest framing for an interview: every row in the left column is real, and every row in the right column is a cost that has to be actively engineered, not one that comes free with the architecture. Teams that adopt micro-frontends and skip the right-column work end up with all the operational overhead and none of the isolation benefit.

slides.sectionTitle: What breaks in production, and the number that matters
slides.markdown:
A concrete failure mode worth naming unprompted: **version skew**. Checkout ships a new shared-state package version; search hasn't updated yet; a user navigates between them and search crashes reading a field the new version renamed. Because deploys are independent, this window can last hours to days — the isolation that helps also means there's no single point where a breaking change is caught before it ships to users, unlike a monorepo's shared CI run.

On the numbers side: teams that adopt module federation at real scale routinely report needing a **contract-testing layer** (verifying a shared dependency or event shape hasn't silently broken a consumer) once past roughly 5–10 independently-deployed micro-frontends — below that, informal Slack coordination between teams is often still viable; above it, it isn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: micro-frontends adopted for org reasons on a codebase too small to need them
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** a company with two frontend teams and one mid-sized app splits it into micro-frontends because the pattern is popular, or because a reorg created two teams and someone assumed separate deploys must follow.

**Why it backfires:** every cost on the previous slide's right column — dependency negotiation, contract testing, duplicated infrastructure, cross-app communication design — is now paid by a team too small to have hit the problem micro-frontends solve. Two teams can usually coordinate a shared release train with a Slack message; that coordination cost is far cheaper than the infrastructure this pattern requires.

**Correct model:** micro-frontends earn their cost at a specific inflection point — roughly double-digit teams, or teams with genuinely mismatched release cadences (one ships hourly, another monthly) — not as a default architecture choice. Below that, a well-organized monolithic SPA with feature-based structure (see [component architecture at scale](component-architecture-at-scale)) gets most of the modularity benefit without the runtime cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Isolation you have to build deliberately
slides.markdown:
"A bad deploy stays isolated" is a claim, not a default — it only holds if specific engineering work is done. Each mounted micro-frontend needs its own error boundary so an unhandled exception in checkout doesn't crash the whole page; global mutable state (a global CSS reset, a `window` property one team mutates) has to be avoided or namespaced, since two independently-built apps sharing an untyped global is exactly the coupling the architecture was meant to remove; and CSS needs real scoping (CSS modules, Shadow DOM, or a strict naming convention) since one team's global stylesheet can silently break another team's mounted UI.

The senior-level point: none of this is free with the architecture — it's a checklist an org has to actively enforce, usually via a platform team, or the isolation promise quietly stops being true.

slides.sectionTitle: Deciding: is this the right tool
slides.markdown:
A short decision checklist worth stating explicitly in an interview: how many teams genuinely need independent release cadence, how mismatched are those cadences today, and is the org willing to fund the ongoing cost (contract testing, a platform team, shared-dependency governance) rather than treating adoption as a one-time project.

If the honest answers are "a handful of teams," "not very mismatched," and "no dedicated ownership planned," the interview-grade answer is to recommend *against* micro-frontends and propose the feature-based monolith instead — naming the trade-off and declining the trendier pattern is a stronger signal than defaulting to it.
